concepts.title: Why a Precipitate Forms
concepts.explanation:
You have used a precipitate as evidence: two clear liquids are mixed, the mixture goes cloudy, and something new has plainly been made. That is a sound piece of reasoning and it leaves the interesting question unanswered. Where does a solid come from, when both things you poured in were liquid and clear?

Start with what a solution is. When a soluble substance dissolves, its particles separate and spread right through the water, in pieces far too small to see - which is why the liquid stays clear. Both liquids you mixed were clear because everything in them was dissolved.

Now mix them. The dissolved particles from one solution meet the dissolved particles from the other, and they can react. The new substance they form is the point: sometimes that product is itself soluble, and it simply dissolves like everything else, and the mixture stays clear with nothing to see. But sometimes the new substance is INSOLUBLE - it will not dissolve in water at all. Having nowhere to go, its particles clump together into solid pieces big enough to scatter light, and the mixture turns cloudy. Left to stand, those pieces settle as a layer at the bottom.

That solid is the precipitate, and the whole sequence is: soluble reactants, a chemical reaction, at least one insoluble product.

So a precipitate is not the appearance of matter out of nowhere. Everything in the cloudiness was already dissolved in one of the two liquids; the reaction simply rearranged it into a substance that water cannot hold.
concepts.example: Colourless silver nitrate solution is added to colourless sodium chloride solution and the mixture goes milky white at once. Silver chloride has formed, and silver chloride is insoluble - so it cannot stay dissolved and comes out as a solid. Filter it and you can weigh the very substance that was invisible a moment before.

concepts.title: What the Air Is Actually Made Of
concepts.explanation:
Air is a mixture, and the proportions in it are worth knowing as numbers rather than as impressions, because almost everyone guesses them wrongly.

Clean dry air is about 78% NITROGEN and about 21% OXYGEN. Those two together are 99% of every breath you take. The remaining 1% is argon, together with a small amount of CARBON DIOXIDE - around 0.04% - and traces of several other gases. Water vapour is left out of those figures deliberately, because it varies enormously: the air over the Indian Ocean holds a great deal and the air over a desert almost none, so the composition of DRY air is quoted to have a fixed thing to compare against.

The surprise for most people is the first figure. Oxygen feels like the important gas, because it is the one we need, so it is natural to assume it is the bulk of the air. It is a fifth. The gas we mostly breathe is nitrogen, and we do nothing with it at all - it goes in and comes straight back out, which is exactly why it is useful for flushing food packaging.

Those proportions are steady but not fixed, and two things change them. NATURAL EMISSIONS add gases without anyone's help: a volcano releases carbon dioxide and sulfur dioxide, decaying vegetation releases methane, and forests take carbon dioxide out. POLLUTION adds them because of what people do - the carbon dioxide from burning fuels, and the sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from engines and industry.

The carbon dioxide figure is the one being watched. 0.04% sounds far too small to matter, and it is the change in that small number, driven by burning, that is altering the climate.
concepts.example: A candle is burned in a sealed jar of air until it goes out, and the water it stands in rises by about a fifth of the jar's volume. The candle used up the oxygen and stopped - and four fifths of the air is still in there, unused, because that part is nitrogen.
